dod_intent_evidence: Army SBIR Phase II ($1.32M, 2023) abstract describes active work with SOCOM teams adapting the FIREFLY platform for GPS-denied subterranean personnel/equipment tracking, integrated with Persistent Systems MPU-5 radios used by Special Forces and an ATAK plug-in.
score_evidence: 'At the conclusion of the Sequential Phase II, we will have a ready-to-deploy, defense-focused version of the FIREFLY system for warfighters' — a hard SBIR clock against a 2-person team → stage_pressure

blind_spots.blind_spot: Fluent in GPS-denied and ATAK, but zero mention of ATO/RMF/CMMC despite integrating with Special Forces radios and SOCOM's networks
blind_spots.operator_reality: Integrating with a currently-deployed military radio system (Persistent Systems MPU-5) and ATAK means eventually needing an ATO to move past pilot; no compliance language visible at Sequential Phase II stage is a real risk to the transition clock
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: team's core competency and prior track record is firefighter/industrial safety software, not government network compliance — this is new terrain for them
blind_spots.evidence_quote: we have integrated FIREFLY devices with currently deployed military radio systems such as the Persistent Systems MPU-5 radios used by Special Forces teams

blind_spots.blind_spot: No discussion of battery life or power logistics for 'small, lightweight location-aware tags' and 'field-deployable anchors' across a subterranean mission
blind_spots.operator_reality: SWaP-C matters most exactly where they're deploying — multi-entrance tunnel systems on a SOCOM mission profile; a tag or anchor that dies mid-mission breaks the accountability system at the worst moment
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: abstract focuses on localization accuracy and miniaturized AoA-capable device design, not sustainment/power budget over mission duration
blind_spots.evidence_quote: The FIREFLY system consists of small, lightweight location-aware tags that enable real-time tracking using field-deployable anchors

blind_spots.blind_spot: The system relies on 'an analytical hub' for visualization and processing — unclear if this hub assumes connectivity back to a central point
blind_spots.operator_reality: GPS-denied is not the same as comms-denied; a subterranean, multi-entrance tunnel environment plausibly denies both, and if the 'analytical hub' needs a live link to function, that's the same architecture assumption that broke the 30fps crowd-detection deployment
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: abstract emphasizes the tag/anchor hardware and ATAK visualization, with the hub's connectivity model left unspecified
blind_spots.evidence_quote: as well as an analytical hub and ATAK-based visualization application that enables unprecedented localization visibility in GPS-denied areas

opener_hook: Namatad's Sequential Phase II SBIR is adapting its firefighter FIREFLY platform for SOCOM's subterranean GPS-denied tracking — worth asking how the analytical hub holds up when comms are denied too, not just GPS.
what_they_do: Builds FIREFLY (incident/personnel accountability), CrossCheck (controlled-work safety), and CANAIRY (exposure monitoring) — a location-and-accountability platform originally for firefighters, now adapted under an Army SBIR for SOCOM personnel/equipment tracking in GPS-denied subterranean environments.
